frontend.prompt:
Scope (frontend only):
- UI list pages, counts, item detail/views, item edit (PUT), create/new item forms, delete action/button, client API layer, cache/state management, and automated tests for those areas.

High-level summary of required frontend behavior changes (do not assume backend details beyond the requirements):
- The API will expose a new nullable `deleted_at` property on public item responses (nullable ISO 8601 / RFC3339 UTC string).
- DELETE is now a soft delete on the backend (sets `deleted_at` to an RFC3339 UTC timestamp); creating/migrating existing items sets `deleted_at` to null.
- List endpoints and count now exclude items with `deleted_at != null` (so deleted items will not appear in list responses nor in count responses).
- GET and PUT on items that have been soft-deleted will return 404.
- Authorization semantics are unchanged: unauthorized actions still produce 403; authorized repeated delete of an already-deleted item returns 404; the first delete still returns the same success response/behavior as today.

Concrete frontend implementation tasks:
1) Types / Models
   - Add a nullable `deleted_at: string | null` field to the client-side item type/interface (document: value is RFC3339 UTC string when present; otherwise null).
   - Ensure serializers/parsers accept and preserve `deleted_at` without transforming its semantics.

2) API client
   - Parse and expose `deleted_at` on all item responses (list, get, create, update).
   - For list and count responses: do not locally filter items by `deleted_at` (the backend already excludes deleted items). Rely on server responses for authoritative lists/counts.
   - DELETE call: preserve the existing success condition/handling logic exactly as currently implemented for a first delete (do not change what you treat as a success response). After success, invalidate caches (see below).
   - Error handling: explicitly map HTTP 404 and 403 conditions from GET/PUT/DELETE to different UI behaviors (see sections below). Do not invent intermediate status codes or new response structures.

3) UI behavior and UX
   - Lists and counts:
     - After a successful delete, remove the item from the visible list and ensure the displayed count is re-synchronized with the server: either re-fetch the list and count from the server or invalidate and refresh the relevant caches so counts come from the server (preferred to avoid drift).
     - Do not attempt to show deleted items in lists because backend excludes them.
   - Delete button / flow:
     - Keep the existing first-delete success UX (message/notification) exactly as-is. Do not change the message text or success handling logic for the first successful delete call.
     - Disable the delete button while the delete request is in flight to prevent double submission.
     - If the delete request returns 403, show the existing “forbidden/permission” error flow (no silent state changes; keep the item visible).
     - If the delete request returns 404 (authorized user attempting to delete an already-deleted item), treat this as “not found / already deleted” and: remove the item from the UI list if present, clear caches for the item, and show an informative not-found message (use existing not-found UI or message pattern). Do not treat this as a permission error.
   - Item detail and edit (GET / PUT):
     - If GET for an item returns 404, show the item-not-found UI (or redirect back to the list) and ensure any local cache for that item is invalidated.
     - If PUT (save/update) returns 404, present not-found feedback (prevent further edits) and invalidate caches; do not convert 404 into a permission error.
     - If PUT returns 403, present permission/forbidden feedback (existing flow) and keep the current UI state.
   - Showing deleted_at:
     - Where item details are displayed, add a read-only field/place to surface `deleted_at` when present (nullable). If `deleted_at` is null, show nothing or an explicit “not deleted” state only if that fits current UI patterns; otherwise hide the field. Do not change the model semantics: it is informational only.

4) Caching / state invalidation
   - On successful delete: invalidate any caches or stored state for the deleted item and for list/count endpoints, then re-fetch or rely on cache population to get the up-to-date list and count.
   - On GET/PUT/DELETE 404 responses: invalidate caches for that item and related list/count caches so UI reflects the exclusion of the deleted item.
   - Do not implement local client-side filtering of deleted items; server is the source of truth.

5) Concurrency and optimistic updates
   - If the client currently uses optimistic removal of items on delete, keep doing so only if you continue to treat the same first-delete success condition as success. Immediately disable the delete control while request is in flight to avoid duplicate deletes.
   - If an optimistic update has already removed an item and the delete request fails with 404, simply ensure final state matches server: remove the item (already removed) and show a not-found message if needed; if it fails with 403, restore item in UI and show forbidden feedback.

6) Tests and QA
   - Unit tests (API client, reducers/store, components): add test cases covering:
     - Parsing `deleted_at` as nullable.
     - List endpoints do not return deleted items (validate UI handles an empty/updated list correctly).
     - Count value matches API and updates after delete.
     - Delete flow: first successful delete still produces the same success-handling behavior; ensure the delete button is disabled while request in-flight; ensure caches are invalidated.
     - Authorized repeat-delete returns 404 → UI shows not-found and removes item.
     - GET and PUT returning 404 → UI shows not-found and invalidates caches.
     - 403 responses continue to map to forbidden/permission-denied UI and do not remove items.
   - Integration / E2E tests:
     - Scenario: authorized user deletes item → list no longer shows item and count decreased (or matches server response after re-fetch).
     - Scenario: authorized user deletes same item again → client receives 404 → item is absent and not-found message shown.
     - Scenario: unauthorized user attempts delete → receives 403 → item remains and forbidden feedback is shown.
     - Scenario: user opens edit page, item is deleted by another actor, GET returns 404 → edit UI shows not-found and redirects or closes editor.

7) Acceptance criteria (must be verified in QA):
   - The original delete permission model is preserved: attempts without permission still produce 403 and the UI shows the forbidden behavior exactly as before.
   - The first successful delete still triggers the same success message/handling as prior behavior.
   - An authorized attempt to delete an already-deleted item results in a 404 and the UI treats it as not-found (item removed from list if present, not a permission error).
   - Lists and counts exclude deleted items (validated by re-fetch after delete or by test server responses).
   - GET and PUT on deleted items return 404 and the UI responds by showing not-found and invalidating caches.
   - Public item responses include a nullable `deleted_at` and the frontend safely exposes it in the item detail UI without changing business rules.

Implementation notes / constraints (do not assume undocumented backend changes):
- Do not invent or rely on any response fields beyond `deleted_at` and standard HTTP status codes and messages mentioned above.
- Preserve existing delete success detection/handling logic exactly; if code currently checks for particular HTTP status codes for success, keep that check unchanged for first-delete behavior.
- Avoid client-side heuristics that try to infer server-side deletion state beyond the documented behaviors; rely on HTTP status codes and server responses.

Deliverables for frontend team:
- Code changes: types/interfaces, API client parsing, UI components (list, detail, edit), delete control behavior, caching/invalidation logic.
- Tests: unit and E2E tests described above.
- QA checklist implementing the acceptance criteria.

If you need exact endpoint names, HTTP status mappings, or current delete success status code to preserve success-detection logic, fetch those from the existing frontend API client code (do not assume them in these instructions).

backend.prompt:
Scope: implement soft-delete for the backend resource collection(s) described.

Do not change authorization rules. Implement only the backend changes required to satisfy the requirements below.

Requirements to implement
- Replace hard DELETE semantics with soft-delete: DELETE sets a deleted_at timestamp (UTC, RFC 3339) rather than removing the row.
- New records must have deleted_at = null.
- Migrate all existing rows so deleted_at = null.
- List endpoints must exclude rows with deleted_at != null. The count endpoint must apply the same exclusion.
- GET and PUT for a resource that has deleted_at != null must return 404.
- Public resource responses (single and list item representations) must include a nullable deleted_at field. For active resources this field must be null.
- Authorization: preserve existing delete permission. Behavior:
  - If the caller lacks permission for an operation on an existing resource, return 403 as before.
  - If caller is authorized and attempts to DELETE an already-deleted resource, return 404.
  - First successful DELETE must return the same HTTP status and response body/message that the system previously returned for hard deletes.

Implementation checklist (backend engineers)
1) Database schema
  - Add a nullable deleted_at column to each affected table. Prefer a timezone-aware column type where available (e.g., Postgres timestamptz). Example SQL (Postgres):
      ALTER TABLE my_table ADD COLUMN deleted_at timestamptz NULL;
  - Ensure default for new rows is NULL (typical if column is added NULLABLE). Do not set a default of now().
  - Create a partial index to speed queries for non-deleted rows. Example (Postgres):
      CREATE INDEX idx_my_table_active ON my_table (id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
    Adjust index columns according to common filter/sort patterns (e.g., created_at, other search fields).
  - Review unique constraints: if uniqueness should only apply to active rows, change unique indexes to partial unique indexes WHERE deleted_at IS NULL. Do not remove business-required uniqueness — consult product if ambiguous.

2) Data migration / backfill
  - Backfill existing rows to deleted_at = NULL where missing. Example SQL:
      UPDATE my_table SET deleted_at = NULL WHERE deleted_at IS DISTINCT FROM NULL;
    (If adding column defaults to NULL, explicit backfill may not be necessary; still run a check to confirm.)
  - Run migration during maintenance window if needed; ensure zero-downtime patterns (add column NULLABLE first, deploy code that tolerates column, then backfill and add indexes).

3) Model / ORM / repository layer
  - Add a deleted_at property to the domain model and DTOs (nullable).
  - Change repository queries that read active resources to include WHERE deleted_at IS NULL. Examples:
      - FindById(id) used by GET/PUT/DELETE should return only rows where deleted_at IS NULL when the caller expects live resources. For cases where code needs to detect if a row exists but is deleted, provide a repository method that can return row regardless of deleted_at.
      - List and Count operations must include WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.
  - For uniqueness checks and create/update flows, ensure they consider only active rows when required.

4) Service / business logic
  - DELETE handler logic (pseudocode):
      1. Authenticate caller.
      2. Authorize caller for delete on target resource; if unauthorized return 403 (unchanged).
      3. Attempt an atomic update that sets deleted_at only if resource is still active. Use an UPDATE ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL and id = X pattern (or equivalent ORM optimistic check):
           UPDATE my_table
           SET deleted_at = (current UTC timestamp)
           WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL;
         If rows affected == 1 => this is the first delete: respond with the original success status and body (preserve existing message/status for compatibility).
         If rows affected == 0:
           - Determine whether the resource exists at all:
               - If resource does not exist (no row at all) => return 404.
               - If resource exists but deleted_at IS NOT NULL => return 404 (this covers "authorized repeated delete returns 404").
         Note: perform authorization check before the update so unauthorized callers get 403 even for deleted resources.
      4. Ensure the deleted_at value written is the current UTC time formatted/stored consistently. If storing as a timestamp-with-timezone, use DB now() at UTC; if storing as string, format using RFC3339 with Z (example: 2023-01-02T15:04:05Z).
  - Concurrency: rely on UPDATE ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL and check affected rows. This ensures exactly one successful first-delete and others detect already-deleted.

5) GET/PUT handlers
  - For GET and PUT endpoints that return or modify a single resource, implement behavior:
      - First authorize the caller as before for the action that would be performed on an existing resource (e.g., read/update). If unauthorized for an existing resource, return 403.
      - Query for the resource with a filter deleted_at IS NULL.
          - If not found, return 404.
      - Proceed as normal for active resources.
  - Do NOT return deleted resources even to authorized users via GET/PUT.

6) List and Count endpoints
  - Modify all list queries and count queries to add WHERE deleted_at IS NULL so results and counts exclude soft-deleted items.
  - Ensure pagination and cursor behavior remains consistent after filtering.

7) API response contract
  - Add a nullable field deleted_at to all public resource representations (JSON payloads), with null for active resources. Example JSON value when resource is deleted (RFC3339): "deleted_at": "2025-10-03T12:34:56Z".
  - For active resources returned in lists and single-item GETs, set "deleted_at": null.
  - Do not include deleted resources in lists; deleted_at will therefore normally be null in list responses but must still be present in the schema.
  - Do not change other response fields or status codes except as required by the new 404 behavior for deleted resources and the unchanged 403 behavior for unauthorized access.

8) Tests to add / update
  - Unit tests for repository:
      - Query by id returns null when deleted_at != null if using active-only finder.
      - Update-set-deleted_at executes only once (simulate concurrent updates where only first update affects one row).
  - Integration / API tests:
      - DELETE as authorized user on active resource: returns the exact original success HTTP status and body.
      - DELETE as authorized user on already-deleted resource: returns 404.
      - DELETE as unauthorized user on existing resource: returns 403.
      - GET/PUT on deleted resource (authorized): returns 404.
      - GET/PUT on resource when unauthorized: returns 403 for existing active resources as before.
      - List endpoint excludes deleted resources and the returned count matches the filtered count.
      - Create endpoint returns deleted_at = null in response and stored value is null.
      - Migration: after running migrations/backfill, verify all existing rows have deleted_at = null.

9) Logging and audit
  - Log deletion operations with actor, resource id, and timestamp. Do not expose logs to clients; use for audit and troubleshooting.
  - Optionally record who performed the delete in audit logs if available in existing infrastructure; do not add persistent schema columns unless product requests.

10) Backwards compatibility & rollout
  - Perform changes in safe sequence for zero-downtime deployment:
      a) Add nullable deleted_at column and indexes (DB migration).
      b) Deploy code changes that write deleted_at on DELETE but still tolerate missing column if older DB snapshot exists.
      c) Backfill values and add/adjust indexes as needed.
      d) Deploy code changes that enforce excluding deleted rows and that add deleted_at to responses.
  - Keep the original DELETE success HTTP status and message for the first delete for client compatibility.

11) Monitoring and metrics
  - Add monitoring for: number of soft-deletes, rate of attempted deletes on already-deleted resources (could indicate client bugs), and any increase in list query latency due to added filters.

12) Edge cases and clarifications (do not assume beyond these rules)
  - Do not change who can see or modify resources except that deleted resources are no longer returned by GET/PUT and lists.
  - If business rules require restoration (undelete) later, implement as a separate operation with explicit product approval; do not add restore behavior now.
  - If there are batch delete APIs, apply the same atomic update pattern per item and return per-item results consistent with single-item DELETE semantics.

Deliverables
- DB migration scripts (add column, backfill, indexes; optional partial unique indexes if required).
- Repository/ORM changes to include deleted_at and to implement active-only finders.
- Service-layer changes implementing the DELETE atomic update pattern and GET/PUT behavior.
- API changes to include nullable deleted_at in responses and to return 404 for deleted resources.
- Automated tests covering the behaviors listed above.
- Deployment instructions: migration first, then code, with rollout plan and monitoring.

Acceptance criteria
- New and migrated records have deleted_at = null.
- DELETE sets deleted_at to the current UTC RFC3339 timestamp and returns the original success message for the first delete.
- Authorized repeated DELETE on already-deleted resource returns 404.
- Unauthorized operations on existing resources return 403 as before.
- GET and PUT on deleted resources return 404.
- List and count exclude deleted rows.
- Public resource responses include a nullable deleted_at field formatted in RFC3339 (UTC) or null.

Notes
- Where DB-specific SQL is needed, prefer timezone-aware timestamp types (timestamptz) or store ISO8601 UTC strings; ensure consistent formatting on reads (RFC3339 with Z).
